item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — High quantitative threshold.** Recovery of 10,000 metric tons or less per year is outside the prohibition, allowing substantial mining to continue and potentially permitting companies to treat the first 10,000 tons as lawful.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Vessel-by-vessel measurement.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” an operator could divide one mining project among multiple vessels, each recovering no more than 10,000 metric tons.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Per year” is undefined.** The bill does not specify calendar, fiscal, license, or rolling years, creating opportunities to manipulate reporting periods and uncertainty about when a violation begins.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — No aggregation among related parties.** The bill does not combine recovery by affiliates, contractors, joint ventures, or commonly controlled operators, allowing projects to be fragmented among nominally separate companies.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Boundary exclusions.** “More than 10,000” excludes exactly 10,000 metric tons, while “depths greater than 200 meters” excludes mining at exactly 200 meters and all shallower seabeds, regardless of ecological harm.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Unclear geographic scope.** “Seabed” is not limited to the ocean or defined by reference to U.S. waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or areas beyond national jurisdiction. This creates uncertainty about both the bill’s coverage and its extraterritorial reach.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** Companies could argue that test collection, excavation, pumping, stockpiling on the seabed, or lifting material only partway through the water column is not “recovery.”

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — Ancillary mining activities may remain lawful.** Prospecting, drilling, dredging, sediment removal, waste discharge, processing, transport, and construction of seabed infrastructure may not themselves constitute recovery, even when they cause comparable damage or are indispensable to a mining project.

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Commercial” is not independently defined.** It is unclear whether the term requires sale, profit, commercial intent, or merely satisfaction of the quantity test, inviting disputes over pilot projects and operations nominally characterized as research.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — “The Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never specifies which Cabinet secretary has authority to make comparability determinations.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — Coverage depends on an affirmative determination.** A harmful activity outside subparagraph (A) apparently remains legal unless and until the Secretary specifically determines that it poses comparable risks.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — No determination procedure or standard.** The bill supplies no deadlines, evidentiary criteria, rulemaking process, public-notice requirements, or emergency authority, and “risks … comparable” is undefined. This makes determinations slow, inconsistent, and vulnerable to vagueness or arbitrary-and-capricious challenges.

13. **Section 2(2) — “U.S. person” is underinclusive.** The definition omits permanent residents, partnerships, trusts, associations, unincorporated entities, and potentially LLCs, as well as corporations organized under federal, territorial, tribal, District of Columbia, or foreign law.

14. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries and controlled entities are excluded.** A U.S. company or citizen could conduct mining through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary, affiliate, joint venture, or shell company unless its own conduct qualifies as “engaging in” the mining.

15. **Section 2(3) — Covered-vessel threshold is easily evaded.** Vessels of exactly or less than 5,000 gross tons need not register, allowing operators to use fleets of smaller vessels even though those vessels may collectively support a major mining operation.

16. **Section 2(3) — Vessel criteria are ambiguous.** The bill does not identify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement system or define when a vessel is “equipped for” recovery, so operators could remove, lease, or characterize equipment to avoid registration.

17. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is undefined.** The prohibition may not clearly reach financing, insuring, owning, controlling, directing, contracting for, assisting, attempting, conspiring to conduct, or knowingly providing vessels and equipment for mining.

18. **Section 3(a) — Territorial jurisdiction is unclear.** “Any person in the United States” could refer to a person’s physical presence, residence, place of incorporation, or conduct occurring within U.S. territory. The bill also does not expressly cover foreign vessels or foreign entities operating in U.S. waters or from U.S. ports.

19. **Section 3(a) — No responsibility for controlled operations.** Parent companies, beneficial owners, officers, and vessel owners are not expressly liable for mining carried out by subsidiaries, charterers, contractors, or agents.

20. **Section 3(b) — Existing-license exemption swallows the prohibition.** It exempts “mining” conducted under an “exploration license,” potentially converting an exploration authorization into an unlimited exemption for commercial extraction.

21. **Section 3(b) — Qualifying licenses are not identified.** The bill does not say whether the license must have been issued by NOAA, another U.S. authority, a foreign government, or the International Seabed Authority. An operator could claim coverage based on virtually any pre-enactment instrument labeled an exploration license.

22. **Section 3(b) — The grandfather clause lacks limits.** It has no expiration date, geographic boundary, production cap, environmental conditions, or restriction on renewal, amendment, transfer, expansion, or acquisition of the license after enactment.

23. **Section 3(c) — Environmental-assessment exception is purpose-based and unlimited.** An operator could characterize destructive test mining or bulk sampling as being conducted “for the purpose” of assessment, with no tonnage cap or requirement that assessment be the sole or primary purpose.

24. **Section 3(c) — No approval or safeguards for assessment activities.** The exception requires no permit, independent scientific review, environmental standards, monitoring, data disclosure, restoration, or showing that the activity is necessary and minimally damaging.

25. **Section 4(a) — Registration timing and procedures are missing.** The bill provides no registration deadline, renewal requirement, required information, change-of-ownership rule, public registry, or express authority for NOAA to issue implementing regulations.

26. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, chartering, management, and operational control may rest with different parties, allowing each to dispute responsibility for registration and reporting.

27. **Section 4 — Registration does not establish authorization.** The bill does not state that registration is merely informational and not permission to mine, creating a risk that operators will portray registration as federal approval or a safe harbor.

28. **Section 4(b) — Reporting requirements are too vague.** “Describing the recovery activities” does not expressly require quantities, minerals, dates, coordinates, depths, methods, affiliated vessels, environmental impacts, customers, or the legal basis for any claimed exemption.

29. **Section 4(b) — Reporting periods and filing deadlines are unspecified.** “Quarterly” does not establish when quarters begin, when reports are due, how inactive quarters are handled, or how corrections must be made.

30. **Section 4(b) — Certification is weak and unclear.** The bill does not specify who must certify, what the certification must state, or that it must be made under penalty of perjury after reasonable inquiry.

31. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no express penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register, failure to report, and false or incomplete reporting under section 4 are not enforceable under the Act.

32. **Sections 4 and 5 — No recordkeeping, inspection, or audit powers.** NOAA is not authorized to demand underlying records, inspect vessels or equipment, audit reports, use vessel-monitoring systems, issue subpoenas, or require preservation of evidence.

33. **Section 5 — No enforcement authority or process is designated.** The bill does not identify the agency that assesses civil penalties, the Attorney General’s role, the applicable hearing and judicial-review procedures, venue, limitations period, or standards governing penalty amounts.

34. **Section 5(a) — Civil penalties may be an inadequate cost of doing business.** The maximum is assessed only per day, rather than per vessel, ton, act, or violation, and the bill provides no minimum, disgorgement of profits, or adjustment for inflation.

35. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” may create an unnecessarily high burden.** Defendants may argue that prosecutors must prove knowledge not merely of the conduct but also of the prohibition or its application, especially given the bill’s ambiguous definitions and exemptions.

36. **Section 5 — Essential remedies are absent.** The bill does not expressly authorize injunctions, immediate cease-and-desist orders, permit suspension, vessel detention, forfeiture, impoundment, cleanup or restoration orders, remediation damages, or recovery of enforcement costs.

37. **Section 5 — No liability allocation or anti-evasion rule.** The bill does not provide joint and several liability, successor liability, liability for corporate officers who direct violations, or veil-piercing rules for shell companies.

38. **Section 5 — No citizen-suit or petition mechanism.** If the responsible administration declines to enforce the Act or make a section 2(1)(B) determination, affected communities and conservation organizations have no express means to compel action.

39. **Section 6 — The international mandate is largely precatory.** Requiring the Secretary of State to “seek to negotiate” demands neither completion of negotiations nor submission, ratification, implementation, or enforcement of an agreement.

40. **Section 6 — The 18-month deadline is ambiguous.** It is unclear whether negotiations must begin or conclude within 18 months, and there is no reporting requirement or consequence for missing the deadline.

41. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” imports the domestic loopholes.** An agreement equivalent to section 3 could reproduce its thresholds, grandfather clause, environmental-assessment exception, and narrow definition of covered persons rather than establish a comprehensive prohibition.

42. **Section 7(a) — Termination standard is undefined.** “Without serious harm” provides no definition of harm, acceptable risk, time horizon, geographic scale, burden of proof, or precautionary standard.

43. **Section 7(a) — National Academies process is incomplete.** The bill does not require or fund a report, identify who commissions it, establish scientific criteria or conflicts rules, set a deadline, or require the report actually to conclude that mining can occur without serious harm.

44. **Section 7(a) — “Acting on a report” is ambiguous.** Congress could arguably terminate the prohibition after merely considering a report, even if the report concludes that safe mining is impossible.

45. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution procedure is missing.** The bill provides no required text, referral process, timetable, expedited procedure, or express presentment requirement, creating uncertainty over what legislative action satisfies the provision.

46. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — Direct internal contradiction.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes the specified finding, but subsection (b) automatically terminates the entire Act after 10 years even if Congress makes no finding and mining remains unsafe.

47. **Section 7(b) — Sunset terminates more than the prohibition.** Because the entire Act ceases to have effect, the definitions, registry, reporting duties, international mandate, and enforcement provisions also disappear; the text does not expressly preserve pending investigations, penalties, or remedies for pre-sunset violations.

48. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — Effective-date inconsistency.** Section 5 refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the entire Act—including section 3’s prohibition—for 180 days. The mismatch creates avoidable uncertainty about obligations and enforcement during that period.

49. **Sections 3(b) and 8 — Grandfathering cutoff precedes effectiveness.** Licenses are grandfathered based on the enactment date, but the prohibition begins 180 days later, potentially encouraging rushed operations, transfers, amendments, or disputes over licenses obtained during the gap.

50. **Act-wide — No implementing-rule deadline or savings clause.** The Act neither directs agencies to issue regulations by a fixed date nor states that the prohibition is enforceable without regulations; it also lacks severability and savings provisions to protect the remainder of the law or accrued enforcement if one provision is invalidated or the Act sunsets.
